new_statements.quote: The information on stress is very fragmentary, and is not in complete agreement with what is known of stress in Barbareño. [...] Examples of final stress include /ʔɨhɨy-ʔ/ ʔɨhɨ́y 'man, male'; /k-oqloyloy/ koqloylóy 'I am chewing'; /s-axta-kʰɨt/ saxtakʰɨ́t 'the wind is blowing'. [...] Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable. /k-yal-weʔ/ kyáweʔ 'I go [there] to sleep'; /ma-k-ʔap/ mákap 'my house'; /ʔoyon-it-ʔ/ ʔoyónit 'help me!' [...] While there are many cases of penultimate stress, there are also examples of antepenultimate stress as well, occasionally in the same form. /s-aqunimak/ saqunímak ~ saqínimak 'he hides'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Ineseño, primary stress is by default on the penultimate syllable of the word (assigned late, after sandhi and glottal infixation); a handful of forms carry final stress (possibly a lexically stressed stem -kʰɨt), and some Harrington transcriptions mark the antepenult; Applegate stresses that the record is fragmentary. Sister languages held held by the project: Ventureño (Applegate 1973 sec. 226) penultimate after all phonological rules with a few stems bearing distinctive stem-final stress; Barbareño (Wash 1995:71-73, Wash 2001:33, following Harrington 33:0235) weight-sensitive -- penult unless both of the last two syllables are heavy, or the final coda is glottalized, or the final onset is h, in which case final. Applegate's Ineseño final-stress examples (ʔɨhɨ́y, saxtakʰɨ́t) fit the Barbareño rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any of the Chumashan sources opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Ineseño: final-stressed forms ʔɨhɨ́y, koqloylóy, saxtakʰɨ́t, qʰutikʰɨ́tuswun (stem -kʰɨt perhaps lexically stressed); antepenultimate saqunímak ~ saqínimak, saxtipánowon, swatílipin, pamaníkitwon; Beeler's observation (quoted p.13) that many Barbareño words show no prominent syllable. Ventureño: a few stems with distinctive stem-final stress (waqšík, c̓ohóy, xalašát, qaláw). Barbareño: rare lexical exceptions kimí 'even', šayké 'because', and the weight/glottalization/h conditions above.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from J. P. Harrington's field transcriptions (stress marked only sporadically). Applegate notes that when stress is marked for the phrase after external-sandhi elision it usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase as a whole (kšaminínoʔ 'I know'), i.e. stress is assigned by a very low-level post-sandhi rule; intonation contours (vocative, yes-no question) treated separately in sec. 228.
new_statements.identity_note: chum1264 is not a language: ISO 639-3 change request 2008-030 (downloaded, retired [chs] Chumash on 2009-01-16 because 'Chumash is actually a family name, not a language name', and Glottolog 5.3 carries chum1264 only as a Bookkeeping entry with zero descriptive references. The six member languages are Barbareño barb1263 [boi] (already in the catalog: Wash 2001:33, weight-sensitive), Ineseño/Samala ines1240 [inz] (Applegate 1972 sec. 227 -- the statement quoted here), Ventureño vent1242 [veo] (Applegate 1973 sec. 226, held), Purisimeño puri1259 [puy], Obispeño obis1242 [obi] and Cruzeño/Island Chumash cruz1243 [crz] (no first-hand stress statement found; family-level second-hand Mithun 1999 'Stress is usually penultimate' only). The quoted statement therefore belongs to ines1240, not to chum1264; per the code-currency rule a retired family code should get no catalog row of its own -- the catalog candidates are ines1240 (Applegate 1972) and vent1242 (Applegate 1973), both already checked under their own glottocodes today.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees with another about the variety it describes. Wash 2001 (Barbareño) gives a weight-sensitive rule (penult if either of the last two syllables is open; final if both closed, or if the final consonant is glottalized or the final onset aspirated); Applegate 1972 (Ineseño, existing statement) gives 'usually penultimate' with a few final- and antepenultimate-stressed forms and explicitly says the fragmentary Ineseño record is 'not in complete agreement with what is known of stress in Barbareño'; Applegate 1973 (Ventureño) gives penultimate after phonological rules with a few distinctively final-stressed stems. These are different member languages, so the differences are cross-language, not contradictions. Henry 2012 could not be opened, so the Ventureño side has only Applegate 1973.

sources.note: sec. 227 'Stress', ms pp.13-15 (PDF 19-21): information 'very fragmentary'; 'Stress is usually on the penultimate syllable'; a few final-stressed forms (ʔɨhɨ́y, koqloylóy, saxtakʰɨ́t; stem -kʰɨt perhaps lexically stressed); some antepenultimate cases; Beeler reports Barbareño penult with a small set of final-stressed words and often no prominent syllable; phrase stress after external sandhi tends to phrase-penult. Also sec. 286.37 p.137: penultimate stress assigned after glottal infixation.
